content: Tonsillitis is an infection of the tonsils, which are lymphoid tissues located at the back of the throat. This condition often, but not always, results in a sore throat and fever. There are three primary types of tonsillitis: acute, subacute, and chronic. Acute tonsillitis can be caused by either bacterial or viral pathogens, with viral infections accounting for approximately 75% of cases. Subacute tonsillitis, which persists for a duration of three weeks to three months, is typically caused by the bacterium Actinomyces. Chronic tonsillitis, on the other hand, is a long-lasting condition that is almost always bacterial in origin if left untreated. The pathophysiology of tonsillitis involves infection, but it remains unclear whether the swelling and associated symptoms are directly caused by the infectious agents themselves or by the host's immune response to these pathogens. It is also hypothesized that tonsillitis may result from abnormal immune responses to the normal bacterial flora of the nasopharynx. The diagnosis of tonsillitis involves a thorough history and evaluation of symptoms. Common symptoms include a severe sore throat, which may radiate as referred pain to the ears, painful or difficult swallowing (dysphagia), headache, fever, and chills. Patients may also experience a change in their voice, often described as a hot potato voice. Additionally, there may be visible pus on the tonsils and enlargement or tenderness of the cervical lymph nodes in the neck.
